short: Saraceni - swift cavalry from the Saraceni, one of the three biggest Arab tribes known in the 4th century AD. This name later became a generic title for all Arabs. Ammianus Marcellinus, describing the Saracens writes directly: in their raids, they immediately devastated everything they came across, as if ravenous kites, having seen the prey, abduct it with a swift raid. Describing the siege of the Constantinople by the Goths, he adds that from the seizure and sacking the city saved only by a chance: «Shortly before arrived in Constantinople a mounted squad of Saracens (Saracenorum cuneus), suitable rather for robbery raids than for a proper battle. Suddenly seeing a detachment of barbarians, Saracens bravely made a foray out of the city to compete in the battle. The battle lasted for a long time, was intense and both sides dispersed without a decisive result. But the troop of eastern men won the victory in a new and unprecedented manner. One of them, with a mop of hair on his head, naked to the waist, making hoarse ominous sounds, rushed between the Goths with a dagger in his hand. Having slew his enemy, he drew his mouth close to his throat and began to suck the spurting blood. This monstrous scene struck such terror into the barbarians that later they acted, when they had to do something, not with their usual wild courage, but with apparent hesitation».
history: One of the simplest forms of one-armed catapult, the onager relied on twisted skeins of animal sinew which provided the power to hurl either rocks or shot. Inaccurate but powerful, it was an effective siege machine against buildings and fortifications, but was of far less use on the battlefield unless firing into massed infantry ranks. First mentioned by Philon of Byzantium in his treatise on ‘Mechanics’, the onager made use of a sling-like cradle attached to a firing arm. This arm was inserted, twisted, and propelled rocks or shot through torsion. As the firing arm was released, the sling-like cradle would unhook, firing the projectile. A padded beam was incorporated into the housing frame to restrain the arm. Larger machines could require as many as eight or ten crewmen, and the incredible recoil meant that they could not be easily or safely mounted on walls or towers. Quickly constructed wherever wood was readily available, onagers soon became a staple of ancient siege warfare.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
